questions.prompt: What is an algorithm, as this course defines it?
options: The step-by-step logic for solving a problem, independent of any particular programming language
A syntax error caught by the compiler before a program runs
Any block of code written specifically in Apex
A named location in memory that holds a value
questions.explain: An algorithm is the step-by-step logic for solving a problem, independent of any specific language; code is that same logic expressed in a language's exact syntax.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D describes a variable, not an algorithm -- a variable is a named storage location, which is an entirely different concept from the language-independent logic an algorithm represents.

questions.prompt: A developer swaps the two lines below so System.debug runs first. What happens?
options: Nothing changes, since Apex ignores line order
The program runs twice as fast
A compile-time error occurs, because System.debug would reference total before it is ever declared
Apex automatically reorders the lines to fix it
questions.explain: Instructions execute strictly in order. Referencing total before the line that declares and assigns it fails, consistent with the 'Variable does not exist' category of compile-time error.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Apex String literals, like 'Jordan Lee', must be written using ________ quotes, not double quotes.
questions.explain: Apex String values are written with single quotes -- using double quotes instead is a common trip-up for developers coming from languages that use double quotes for strings.

questions.prompt: What does the Apex expression `17 / 5` evaluate to, and why?
options: 4, because Apex rounds up on integer division
3, because dividing two Integer values performs integer division, truncating anything after the decimal point
3.4, because Apex always rounds integer division to one decimal place
An error, because 17 cannot be divided by 5
questions.explain: Dividing two Integer values performs integer division, which truncates the decimal remainder rather than rounding -- 17 / 5 evaluates to 3, not 3.4 or 4.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Apex's `switch on` statement.
options: A single when block can list several comma-separated values that all map to the same block
The when else block, if included, must be the last block in the switch statement
Execution falls through into the next when block unless a break statement stops it
Each when value must be unique
A switch on statement can run more than one matching when block per execution
questions.explain: A when block can list comma-separated values, when else must be last if included, and each when value must be unique. Unlike some other C-family languages, there is no fall-through in Apex's switch -- once a matching block runs, the statement exits, so only one block ever runs.

questions.prompt: Arrange the values of i in the exact order they occur during this loop's execution.
questions.explain: The loop starts i at 0 and runs while i < 3, incrementing after each iteration -- so it runs for i = 0, then i = 1, then i = 2, and stops before i reaches 3.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct definition from this course's first chapter.
right: A loop whose stopping condition never becomes false
The order in which operators are evaluated when more than one appears in an expression
A named location in memory that holds a value a program can refer to and change
The step-by-step logic for solving a problem, independent of any particular language
questions.explain: Algorithm is language-independent logic; a variable is named storage; operator precedence governs evaluation order; an infinite loop never satisfies its own stopping condition.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument, as this course defines them?
options: A parameter is the actual value supplied at a specific method call; an argument is the named placeholder in the method's definition
A parameter is the named placeholder in a method's own definition; an argument is the actual value supplied when the method is called
There is no difference; the two terms are interchangeable
A parameter only applies to static methods, while an argument only applies to instance methods
questions.explain: A parameter is the named placeholder in a method's definition (the blueprint); an argument is the real value supplied at a specific call.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A exactly reverses the two definitions -- it describes an argument where it should describe a parameter, and vice versa.

questions.prompt: A method needs to use one specific Customer object's own loyaltyPoints field to do its job. Per this course, should it be an instance method or a static method?
options: A static method, since static methods are always preferred
A static method, because static methods can access any object's fields automatically
An instance method, since it needs a specific object's own data to do its job
It cannot be either; only constructors can access fields
questions.explain: The rule of thumb: if a method needs a specific object's own data, make it an instance method. A static method belongs to the class itself and doesn't operate on one object's own field values.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in an Apex List, indexing starts at ________, so a List with 5 items has valid indexes 0 through 4.
questions.explain: List indexing is zero-based -- the first item is at index 0, and the last valid index of a List with 5 items is size() - 1, which is 4.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Apex Strings and exceptions, per this course.
options: A String in Apex is immutable -- methods like toUpperCase() return a new String rather than modifying the original
A finally block only runs if an exception was actually thrown inside the try block
A custom exception class is created by extending the built-in Exception class
.split() returns a List<String>
Built-in Apex exception types can be thrown directly by developer code, the same as custom exceptions
questions.explain: Strings are immutable (methods return new Strings), custom exceptions extend the built-in Exception class, and .split() returns a List<String>. A finally block always runs regardless of whether an exception was thrown, and only custom exceptions -- not built-in ones -- can be deliberately thrown by developer code.

questions.prompt: In a try/catch/finally block, what happens to the finally block if no exception was thrown in the try block?
options: It is skipped entirely
It throws its own exception automatically
It only runs if the catch block explicitly calls it
It still runs, since finally always runs after try/catch finishes regardless of outcome
questions.explain: A finally block always runs after the try/catch finishes, whether or not an exception occurred -- making it the right place for cleanup logic that must happen either way.

questions.prompt: Match each Apex collection type to its defining characteristic.
right: Holds key-value pairs, looked up by key rather than position
An ordered collection, indexed from 0, allowing duplicates
An unordered collection with no duplicate values allowed
questions.explain: A List is ordered and allows duplicates; a Set disallows duplicates with no guaranteed order; a Map holds key-value pairs looked up by key.

questions.prompt: Arrange this course's four-step systematic debugging process in the correct order.
questions.explain: The process is: reproduce the bug reliably, isolate which part of the code is responsible, form a specific checkable hypothesis about the cause, and verify that hypothesis before writing a fix.

questions.prompt: Given the error message 'Line: 4, Column: 20 -- Variable does not exist: discountRate', what does this course recommend checking first?
options: Rewrite the entire program from scratch immediately
Search the vague phrase 'my code is broken' online
Look at line 4 specifically, and check spelling and whether discountRate was declared in a scope visible from that line
Ignore the error, since line numbers in Apex error messages are usually inaccurate
questions.explain: The systematic approach is to find the referenced line number and check what the message actually claims against the code -- for 'Variable does not exist,' that means checking spelling and scope.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in version control, a deliberate, labeled checkpoint recording exactly what the code looked like at a moment in time, along with a message describing the change, is called a ________.
questions.explain: A commit is a single labeled snapshot of the codebase with an accompanying message describing what changed and why; a sequence of commits forms the repository's history.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about writing clean code, per this course.
options: DRY means the same underlying logic should exist in exactly one place, not copy-pasted everywhere
Apex convention uses PascalCase for class names and camelCase for variables and methods
A comment that restates exactly what the next line of code already says adds genuine value
Two pieces of code that merely look similar but represent different concepts must always be merged to satisfy DRY
A well-named variable can make an explanatory comment unnecessary
questions.explain: DRY targets duplicated underlying logic, Apex follows PascalCase for classes and camelCase for variables/methods, and a good name can remove the need for a comment. A comment restating the obvious adds nothing, and DRY doesn't require merging merely similar-looking but conceptually different code.

questions.prompt: What minimum percentage of Apex test coverage does Salesforce generally require to deploy code to a production org?
options: There is no minimum requirement
questions.explain: Salesforce generally requires at least 75% Apex test coverage to deploy to a production org -- though this course stresses that chasing the percentage with shallow tests gives a false sense of safety.

questions.prompt: Match each tool or concept to its correct description.
right: A detailed record of what happened during a piece of Apex execution
The underlying tool the Salesforce Extensions for VS Code run on top of
A disposable, source-driven Salesforce environment created for development and testing
A Developer Console window for running a block of Apex immediately without saving it as a class
questions.explain: Execute Anonymous runs Apex immediately without saving a class; a scratch org is a disposable dev/test environment; the Salesforce CLI underlies the VS Code extensions; a debug log records what happened during execution.

questions.prompt: Per this course's closing lesson, why was this entire course taught without requiring a Salesforce org?
options: Because the course's real subject was general programming concepts, taught through Apex's syntax, and that knowledge transfers directly and unchanged into real Apex
Because Salesforce orgs are too expensive to provide to students
Because Apex cannot run inside an actual Salesforce org
Because this course is unrelated to Salesforce development in any way
questions.explain: The course's subject was programming itself -- variables, control flow, functions, classes, collections, exceptions, and developer habits -- all of which transfer directly, unchanged, into real Apex work, which is why no org was ever required.
